prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its bioactive form, which established the incretin axis and made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B010 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case does not rest on the six matching openings. It rests on a chain that is unusually complete: the incretin concept, human physiology of GLP-1 secretion and action, identification of the bioactive truncated peptide, receptor biology and the therapeutic rationale, and then large randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The evidence is mature, independently replicated and unlikely to be overturned. Round 1 sharpened my citation. Several colleagues, notably Wahren-Herlenius and Svenningsson, argued that the citation should not read as if the drugs were an afterthought, and I have moved from 'established the incretin axis that underlies treatment' to wording that says this physiology made incretin-based therapy possible. That is a change of wording, not of configuration.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness and the committee should say so openly. Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group has not been checked against primary papers by any of us, and Habener is not among the credited names, so this ballot cannot offer a substitute. Knudsen is credited on the ballot and is left out only because of the three-person cap and the choice to emphasise discovery; her half-life-extension chemistry is a scientific achievement and not routine development, and the citation should not suggest otherwise. Long-term obesity outcomes and safety are still accumulating, which does not affect the case for the discovery but does mean the clinical story is not finished. If a documentary check showed that Mojsov's contribution was derivative, I would reopen the allocation and not simply keep her name.

responses.point: Perlmann says that if developers are excluded because their work was industrial, the standard must be applied consistently, for example to Bennett in B045, and he would not narrow B006 to June and Sadelain before the Eshhar question is resolved.
responses.response: The consistency point is fair and it is why I do not rest the exclusion of Knudsen on the word industrial. The cap and the emphasis on the discovery that opened the field decide it, and I would accept the same reasoning for B045, where Bennett's work is the drug-making step on top of Krainer's splicing mechanism. I agree with his condition on B006: removing Rosenberg does not repair the missing Eshhar, so I treat B006 as a fallback that carries an unresolved attribution problem and not as a clean second part. That is a further reason I do not add it to B010 as a two-part prize.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius holds that B008 is not ready as a prize part, because channelrhodopsin discovery and neuronal deployment are separate achievements and any three-person cut is contestable, while B010 has a decisive demonstrated human benefit.
responses.response: She has moved me part of the way. In round 1 I argued that a method that opened intractable questions deserves recognition, and I still think the Prize has done that. But she is right that B008 is the weaker fit for a Physiology or Medicine prize today: the credited list has six names, and a molecular-plus-implementation split such as Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth leaves Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck with credible claims. I therefore keep B008 only as a second alternative, behind B006, and I would not pair it with B010. I do not agree that B010's attribution problem is comparable to B008's in structure, since all three of my names sit in one continuous line from physiology to therapy.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B020 third as the cleanest pair, says naming the drugs in the B010 citation would require reconsidering Knudsen at the cost of Mojsov or Drucker, and says the fallback if B010 fails is unclear.
responses.response: I agree that naming the drugs would reopen Knudsen, and I do not want to do that by implication, which is why my citation says the physiology made the therapy possible and does not name semaglutide or liraglutide. On the fallback, I would take B006 first: its clinical record is clear even though the Eshhar gap makes the allocation fragile. B020 is the cleanest attribution, but Perlmann's point stands that PERK and ATF6 lie outside the Walter and Mori core, and its disease relevance is still mostly conceptual, so I keep it off my alternatives. I do not think a cleaner pair should displace a mature discovery with measured outcomes.

responses.point: The chair asks that the Mojsov versus Habener priority check be treated as a precondition and says he and Sandberg would withdraw support if a documentary check showed Mojsov's contribution to be derivative.
responses.response: I share that position and would state the decision rule plainly. We should accept the supplied record only as far as it goes. I would proceed with Mojsov if the primary papers show her group identifying and characterising the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide independently, even if Habener's group was working on the proglucagon sequences in parallel. If the record shows only overlap that cannot be separated, I would not swap in a name the ballot does not supply. I would instead consider whether a two-name B010 prize, Drucker and Holst, with a citation worded around human physiology and receptor biology, still stands. I would not decide that by counting votes.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority over the Habener group survives a check of primary papers and dates; none of us has done it.
Whether a two-name B010 version is defensible if her claim weakens, given that Habener cannot be named from this ballot.
Whether Knudsen should be first reserve if any of the three names weakens, or whether the cap settles her exclusion.
Whether any CAR-T configuration is safe while Eshhar is outside the credited names, which matters because B006 is my first fallback.
statement.conflict_note: I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons and a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, who is not on this committee. Neither connection involves any shortlisted candidate or credited name. As a neuroscientist I use optogenetic tools, and I have not let that raise B008 in my ranking. No recusal is required and this disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
